source_reviews.independent_solution: 在把物体看作质点，或只研究其整体平动的范围内，若一个力对同一物体整体平动的作用效果，与几个力同时作用对该物体整体平动的合成效果相同，这个等效的力就叫作这几个力的合力。合力是这些力的矢量和；它是原有几个力的等效表示，不是额外施加的力。这个平动意义下的等效，不能保证同时完整替代这些力造成的转动或形变。

mathematics.independent_solution: In the stated same-body translation-only scope, the resultant is a single equivalent force whose translational effect matches all the original forces acting simultaneously. Let R = sum(F_i), with every term a vector. Largest-force selection, retaining the originals and adding another force, and cancellation are distinct operations and do not define R. The complete true set is {B}. After the authorized author disclosure, the exact author set and every per-option truth, derivation and misconception were compared; all agree without altering the frozen independent set.

option_checks.evidence: The resultant represents all simultaneously acting forces, not just the largest. For collinear 2 N right and 3 N right, the simultaneous resultant is 5 N right, while this rule represents only 3 N right. A special case in which other forces cancel does not make largest-force selection a general definition. Author-disclosure comparison: The author explicitly selects the largest member and deletes the others. This is the same wrong rule inferred before disclosure; the author's same-direction nonzero example agrees with the frozen 2 N + 3 N versus 3 N counterexample. The stated misconception really produces option A, which is false as a general definition.

Within the stem's same-body translational scope, let R be the vector sum of the original forces. A single equivalent force R has the same translational effect as those forces acting simultaneously. This is exactly the definition frozen in SOURCE2; the option replaces their action rather than adding an actual extra force. Author-disclosure comparison: The author compares one force acting alone with the original forces acting simultaneously on the same body in the translation scope. That matches frozen option B and its independently established equivalence criterion; truth=correct and misconception=null are appropriate.

If the original vector sum is R and the added force is F, retaining the originals gives R + F. Equality to the original effect requires F = 0, not the general resultant F = R. For an original resultant 5 N right, adding its 5 N right equivalent while retaining the originals yields 10 N right, not 5 N right. The zero-force degeneracy does not define a general resultant. Author-disclosure comparison: The author derives S + F = S and F = 0, exactly agreeing with the frozen extra-force/no-change analysis. Its misconception is actual addition while retaining all components, which produces this option rather than a different error. The zero-force coincidence is not promoted to a general resultant definition.

A force cancelling the original translational effect is the equilibrating force -R, not the resultant R. For an original resultant 5 N right, the cancelling force is 5 N left and therefore has the opposite, not the same, individual translational effect. Equality in the zero-resultant special case does not identify cancellation with the general definition. Author-disclosure comparison: The author derives S + F = 0 and F = -S, agreeing with the frozen equilibrant-versus-resultant distinction, opposite directions for nonzero S, and the zero-resultant special-case caveat. This concrete cancelling procedure produces option D and is false as a general resultant definition.

mathematics.independent_solution: Composition means starting with the several simultaneous forces on the same body and finding their equivalent translational resultant R = sum(F_i), accounting for both magnitudes and directions. Adding R to the retained forces double-counts their action; starting from a known force and finding several is decomposition; summing magnitudes and using the largest force's direction is not general vector addition. The complete true set is {D}. After the authorized author disclosure, the exact author set and every per-option truth, derivation and misconception were compared; all agree without altering the frozen independent set.

option_checks.evidence: This is an actual addition of a further force, not finding the resultant of the given forces. With original sum R, retaining every component and adding R produces 2R. An original 5 N right system would become 10 N right. The zero-resultant special case does not turn this extra-force procedure into composition. Author-disclosure comparison: The author computes S + S after retaining all components and adding the equivalent force. This agrees with the frozen 2R analysis and is the exact extra-force procedure stated by option A; the nonzero qualification avoids making a false claim about the zero special case.

The procedure starts with one known force and seeks several forces with the same joint effect: that is decomposition, the reverse direction of the requested operation. For example, starting from 5 N right and seeking 2 N right plus 3 N right decomposes the known force. Composition starts with the given several forces and finds their one equivalent resultant. Author-disclosure comparison: The author identifies one-known-force input and several-equivalent-forces output. This is the same reversed input/output rule independently identified as decomposition in BLIND, and it actually produces option B rather than the requested composition.

Vector addition cannot generally be replaced by a sum of magnitudes and the direction of the largest member. For 3 N right and 2 N left, correct composition gives 1 N right; the stated procedure gives 5 N right. The unique largest force fixes the distractor's direction here, so the discrepancy is not a tie ambiguity. Coincidence for all codirectional forces does not validate the general rule. Author-disclosure comparison: The author adds magnitudes and copies the largest member's direction. Its opposite 3 N and 2 N example gives the same frozen discrepancy, 5 N versus 1 N. The all-codirectional coincidence is explicitly restricted to special cases; the procedure and misconception correspond exactly to option C.

Taking the sizes and directions of all given same-body forces and finding one force with their joint translational effect is finding their vector sum R. This is the requested composition operation. For 3 N right and 2 N left it gives 1 N right, preserving directional cancellation. The stem already supplies the translational restriction and the option does not add another actual force. Author-disclosure comparison: The author starts with simultaneous forces on one body, keeps sizes and directions, and finds one force representing their joint translational effect. This is the same composition operation frozen before disclosure; truth=correct and misconception=null agree with independent option D.
